claims.text: Introducing a nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation, nano-coupled grains, and nanoprecipitates will reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate over a wide temperature range.
The untreated high-entropy alloy has a relatively homogeneous microstructure lacking engineered nanohierarchical features.
Tailored heat treatment and alloying adjustments can induce composition undulations, coupled nanograins, and nanoprecipitates in the alloy.
The intervention will be effective during sliding from room temperature to approximately 800 °C.
The nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates facilitate adaptive friction-interface protection.
At lower temperatures, nanostructural heterogeneity provides multiple deformation pathways that release gradient frictional stress.
At approximately 800 °C, the architecture activates formation of a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer.
The dense nanocrystalline glaze layer minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear.
The cooperative nanohierarchical mechanism lowers the coefficient of friction.
The cooperative nanohierarchical mechanism reduces wear.
The modified alloy will have a statistically significant reduction in coefficient of friction relative to the untreated alloy.
The modified alloy will have a statistically significant reduction in wear rate relative to the untreated alloy across the tested temperature range.
Performance will persist only while the nanohierarchical features remain stable under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading.
Excessive temperature spikes or loads beyond design limits may destabilize the nanoscale features and compromise tribological performance.
